title: Rubella
wiki_lead:
Rubella, also known as German measles or three-day measles, is a vaccine-preventable infection caused by the rubella virus. Symptoms of the disease are often mild, sometimes inapparent. A rash may appear around two weeks after exposure and last for three days, usually starting on the face then spreading to the rest of the body. The rash is sometimes itchy and is not as bright as that of measles. Swollen lymph nodes are common and may last a few weeks. A fever, sore throat, and fatigue may also occur. Joint pain is common in adults. Complications may include bleeding problems, testicular swelling, encephalitis, and inflammation of nerves. Infection during early pregnancy may result in a miscarriage or a child born with congenital rubella syndrome (CRS). Symptoms of CRS manifest as problems with the eyes such as cataracts, deafness, as well as affecting the heart and brain. Problems are rare after the 20th week of pregnancy.
Rubella is usually spread from one person to the next through the air via coughs of people who are infected. People are infectious during the week before and after the appearance of the rash. Infants born with CRS may be infectious for up to a year. Only humans are infected. Insects do not spread the disease. Once recovered, people are immune to future infections. Testing is available that can verify immunity. Diagnosis is confirmed by finding the virus in the blood, throat, or urine. Testing the blood for antibodies may also be useful.
It can be prevented by the rubella vaccine, with a single dose being more than 95% effective. Often it is given in combination with the measles vaccine and mumps vaccine, known as the MMR vaccine. When some, but less than 80%, of a population is vaccinated, more women may reach childbearing age without developing immunity by infection or vaccination, thus possibly raising CRS rates. Once infected, there is no specific treatment.
Rubella is a common infection in many areas of the world. Each year, about 100,000 cases of congenital rubella syndrome occur. Rates of disease have decreased in many areas as a result of vaccination. There are ongoing efforts to eliminate the disease globally. In April 2015, the World Health Organization declared the Americas free of rubella transmission. The name "rubella" is from Latin and means little red. It was first described as a separate disease by German physicians in 1814, resulting in the name "German measles".

Signs and symptoms
Rubella can affect people of any age. Most people catch the infection in childhood, or are vaccinated, and have lifelong immunity thereafter. It is generally a mild disease, and the symptoms may be unnoticeable. However, if a woman becomes infected during early pregnancy the effect on her unborn child can be very severe.
The incubation period - between exposure to the virus, and the appearance of symptoms - ranges from 2 to 3 weeks. Some infections are asymptomatic. During the incubation period, the patient is contagious, typically for about one week before he/she develops a rash and for about one week thereafter.
The most obvious symptom of rubella is a rash, generally starting behind the ears then spreading over the rest of the body; this is less noticeable on persons with dark skin. The fades after a few days, which is why it is sometimes known as three-day measles. Not everybody gets the rash. Other common symptoms, especially in children, include cold-like symptoms (cough, sneezing, headaches, sore throat), swollen lymph glands behind the ear, and a mild fever. Symptoms generally clear after a few days without treatment although the swollen glands can persist for several weeks.
Adults who get the disease may suffer aching joints, arthritis, and bleeding issues caused by destruction of blood platelets.
Encephalitis is a severe but rare complication of rubella.

grok_lead: Rubella, also known as German measles, is a contagious viral infection caused by the rubella virus, a single-stranded RNA virus in the genus Rubivirus of the family Matonaviridae, that primarily affects children and young adults but can occur at any age. The disease is transmitted through respiratory droplets from coughing or sneezing, with humans serving as the only natural hosts, and is most infectious from one week before to about one week after the onset of the characteristic rash. While typically mild, with symptoms including a maculopapular rash starting on the face and spreading to the body, low-grade fever, and posterior auricular lymphadenopathy, approximately 25% to 50% of infections are asymptomatic. The incubation period for rubella averages 17 days (ranging from 12 to 23 days), and the illness usually resolves within three days, earning it the alternative name "three-day measles." Complications are uncommon in children but more frequent in adults, particularly women, who may experience arthralgia or arthritis in up to 70% of cases; rare severe effects include thrombocytopenic purpura or encephalitis. The most significant risk arises during pregnancy, especially in the first trimester, where maternal infection carries a 90% transmission risk to the fetus, potentially leading to congenital rubella syndrome (CRS) in the newborn. CRS is a leading vaccine-preventable cause of birth defects worldwide, affecting an estimated 32,000 infants in 2019 (with modeling suggesting around 36,000 in 2023), with lifelong conditions such as sensorineural hearing loss, congenital cataracts, congenital heart defects, and developmental delays. Diagnosis relies on laboratory confirmation rather than clinical presentation alone, due to similarities with other rash illnesses like measles or parvovirus; methods include polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing of nasopharyngeal swabs, throat swabs, or urine, and serological detection of rubella-specific IgM antibodies. There is no specific antiviral treatment for rubella; management is supportive, focusing on symptom relief, isolation to prevent spread (for seven days after rash onset), and prenatal care for pregnant individuals. Prevention is highly effective through vaccination with the measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine or its MMRV variant, which provides lifelong immunity in over 95% of recipients after one dose and nearly 100% after two doses. The vaccine is recommended in two doses for childrenâat 12 to 15 months and 4 to 6 yearsâand for susceptible adults, particularly those born after 1957 or at risk of exposure. Globally, rubella remains a public health concern despite significant progress; the World Health Organization (WHO) reported 17,865 cases across 78 countries in 2022, a 97% reduction from 670,894 cases in 2000, attributed to expanded immunization programs. As of 2025, 19 countries have not introduced rubella-containing vaccines, accounting for approximately 78% of the global CRS burden. In the United States, rubella was declared eliminated in 2004, with fewer than 10 cases annually, mostly import-related, due to high vaccination coverage exceeding 90%. The WHO's Global Measles and Rubella Strategic Plan aims for elimination in all regions by 2030, with 175 of 194 countries having introduced rubella-containing vaccines by January 2024, achieving 69% first-dose coverage. Continued surveillance and vaccination efforts are essential to prevent outbreaks and reduce the burden of CRS in low-coverage areas.
